text.p: Fears of a widening trade deficit putting pressure on the peso were unfounded as the country's overall economic position was strong, Philippine central bank governor Gabriel Singson said on Thursday.
"As far as the trade deficit is concerned, which could reach $12 billion for the whole of 1996, we do not believe it should be a cause for alarm at this stage," Singson said at a business luncheon.
The underlying factors behind the trade deficit did not suggest either loss of export competitiveness or excessive consumption, he said.
Philippine exports were currently growing at 18 percent annually, which was significantly higher than growth rates in other East Asian countries, Singson said.
"If only for this fact alone, we find it quite ridiculous, as some quarters keep insisting, that the peso should be forced to depreciate allegedly to restore competitiveness," he said.
The government has said the trade deficit was growing because of higher capital goods imports, which was expected in a growing economy.
"The exchange rate, as determined by the market, should be generally left alone except during instances of temporary speculative activity," Singson said.
The peso hit a 27-month low early on Thursday at 26.345 to the dollar. It has been weakening since Tuesday after interest rates fell following last Friday's cut in banks' reserve requirements.
Central Bank Treasurer Sergio Edeza said the Bank sold less than $15 million early on Thursday to stop the peso from further weakening.
He said there was no outflow of foreign funds due to recent declines in domestic interest rates.
"This is partly speculative. There was also profit-taking on certain positions," he said.
Separately, Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo, told Reuters: "If you see the peso going up or down, it is likely because of market forces."
